food.text: Between about 2500 and 1200 BCE, Bantu-speaking farming peoples originally from Nigeria and Cameroon split into two migrating branches. East Bantu farmers moved toward areas such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, while West Bantu farmers settled around Congo and Gabon, carrying agriculture into Central Africa.
Around 2500 BCE, Bantu-speaking migrants had already reached the Great Lakes region of Central Africa. This was part of the broader Bantu Migration that shaped the region.

For thousands of years, the ancestors of Central Africa's Pygmy peoples survived by hunting and gathering in the Congo Basin rainforest rather than growing food. About 3,500 years ago, farming peoples of the Bantu expansion began arriving, and the Pygmies were partially absorbed or displaced by them, adopting their languages. The article says the Pygmy peoples were greatly decimated by this prehistoric Bantu expansion, and that they have been widely affected by enslavement at the hands of neighboring Bantu, Ubangian and Central Sudanic groups ever since.

Bantu-speaking farmers began moving south from sites south of Shum Laka in southern Cameroon and Gabon between about 5000 and 3000 BCE. Without iron tools to clear the dense rainforest, their progress was very slow, and it took until about 1500 BCE for these farming migrants to reach central Cameroon.

As the Western Stream of Bantu farmers pushed south, they likely followed the coast and the rivers of the Congo system, and may even have used the sea to travel. Starting around 2000 BCE, a drier climate began to degrade parts of the West-Central African rainforest, which is thought to have helped clear the way for these farming migrants.

art.text: From the late 3rd millennium BCE, people in the Central African Republic and Cameroon built megaliths, including monuments and cairn burials. They were raised in regions such as Eastern Adamawa, the Oubanguian Ridge and the Chad/Congo watershed.

Seated and crouched chimpanzee statuettes were developed between 2300 BCE and 1500 BCE. Speculatively, these artistic depictions, or the animals themselves, may have travelled through a long-distance trade network into the Near East, for example to Elam.

One period of megalith building in Central African Republic and Cameroon, called Balimbé, ran from 2000 BCE to 1000 BCE. Megaliths were made for various purposes, including ritual practices and territorial marking.

Chimpanzees originate in the savanna and forest of West Africa and Central Africa. By the 2nd millennium BCE, they or their artistic depictions may have been exchanged from those regions toward the Near East, though the source calls this rather speculative.

One proposed route for the chimpanzee statuettes ran from West Africa or Central Africa through East Africa, including the Elmenteitan, and across Arabia. It would have ended in the Near East, in places such as Elam.

Another possibility, suggested by a report of Hanno the Navigator, is a sea route. Chimpanzee statuettes may have travelled by maritime trade from the Gulf of Guinea to the eastern Mediterranean, then along the Incense Route into the Near East.

science.text: In Sub-Saharan Africa, copper metallurgy generally does not come before iron working, so the three-age system fits poorly. Iron metallurgy began in Western and Central Africa by 2500 BC - 1000 BC, and possibly earlier.

Tin is essential for making tin-bronzes, but it is rare, at about two parts per million in the Earth's crust. Its use began in the Middle East and the Balkans around 3000 BC, and central and South Africa are listed among the known ancient sources of tin.
science.source_title: Tin sources and trade during antiquity

science.text: Iron metallurgical development in Central Africa has been dated to 2136 BCE to 1921 BCE at Obui, in the Central African Republic. Another site, Lejja in Nigeria, has been dated to 2631 BCE to 2458 BCE.
According to Augustin Holl (2018), the site of Gbatoro in Cameroon shows evidence of ironworking dated to 2,153–2,044 BCE and 2,368–2,200 BCE.

According to Zagato and Holl, there is evidence of iron smelting in the Central African Republic that may date back to 3000 to 2500 BCE. If correct, ironworking there began during the Bronze Age of other parts of the world.

Augustin Holl (2018) reports evidence of ironworking at Gbatoro, Cameroon, dated to 2,153 to 2,044 BCE and 2,368 to 2,200 BCE. Iron metallurgy at Obui, in the Central African Republic, is dated to 2136 BCE to 1921 BCE.

Archaeometallurgical knowledge is described as having originated in several centers in West, Central and East Africa. Because these centers lie within inner Africa, the developments are described as native African technologies, including iron work in Central Africa at Obui.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Africa

science.text: Radiocarbon and thermoluminescence dating of iron-related artifacts in Nigeria and the Central African Republic have given dates as early as the third millennium BC. Some scholars question the methods behind these dates, while others say they undermine the diffusionist model of how iron metallurgy began in Sub-Saharan Africa.

culture.text: The oral word is revered in most African cultures, and history has predominantly been passed down through oral tradition. Some societies were heterarchical and egalitarian, while others organised into chiefdoms.

Peoples of Central Africa shared common historical processes and widespread movements of people, so their cultures show many similarities. Similar practices appear in music, dance, art, body adornment, initiation, and marriage rituals.

Between around 3000 BCE and 500 CE, the Bantu expansion swept from north-western Central Africa (modern day Cameroon) across much of Central, Eastern, and Southern Africa. It displaced or absorbed groups such as the Khoisan and Pygmies.

Bantu-speaking agriculturalists in the Grasslands of northwestern Cameroon began gradually migrating south sometime between 5000 and 3000 BCE. Researchers still do not know why they moved or which directions they took, though they agree there were multiple dispersal events. Around 1500 BCE, Bantu speakers reached central Cameroon.

Around 2500 BCE, Bantu migrants had reached the Great Lakes Region in Central Africa. They were part of the long movement of Bantu-speaking peoples that would shape the languages and cultures of the region.
